extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners evaluating whether claim additional elements make a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon) into patent-eligible subject matter under the Alice/Mayo Step 2A/Step 2B framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating whether the additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a determination whether the additional elements in a claim amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, the examiner should evaluate whether the elements define only well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points examiners must consider: (1) Being known in the art does not necessarily make an element conventional—novel/obvious inquiries are separate from eligibility (e.g., Enfish illustrates known features can be non-conventional if they provide technical improvements). (2) A factual determination is required to support a conclusion that an additional element (or combination) is well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Berkheimer), but a prior-art search is not always necessary; examiners may rely on what courts or those in the art recognize and on the specification’s own statements. The examiner should conclude based on their expertise that an element is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry; if not, the element will generally favor eligibility (example: glucose-sensing earring vs. routine blood glucose monitoring). The factual determination must be expressly supported in writing (see MPEP § 2106.07(a)); appropriate forms of support include: (a) citation to the specification or applicant statements, (b) citation to relevant court decisions, (c) citation to publications showing conventionality, or (d) official notice by the examiner. (3) Even if individual elements are conventional, their combination may amount to an inventive concept (Diamond v. Diehr; Rapid Litigation; BASCOM). A rejection should be made only if the examiner, relying on expertise, can conclude in Step 2B that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for how to support conclusions on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer functions courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts have recognized certain generic computer functions as well-understood, routine, and conventional functions when recited at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples the courts have treated as routine when claimed generically: (i) receiving or transmitting data over a network (e.g., using the Internet to gather data; utilizing an intermediary computer to forward information); (ii) performing repetitive calculations (e.g., recomputing or readjusting values); (iii) electronic recordkeeping (e.g., creating/maintaining shadow accounts; updating activity logs); (iv) storing and retrieving information in memory; (v) electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document (e.g., OCR); and (vi) a web browser’s back-and-forward button functionality. Caveat: this listing does not mean all computer functions are routine or that a generic computer implementation is necessarily ineligible—cases like DDR Holdings, Amdocs, and BASCOM show that specific arrangements or technical improvements can render claims eligible. Courts have found ineligible claims where the claim as a whole is nothing more than generic computer functions implementing an abstract idea (human-analog). Conversely, eligible claims can arise when generic components in combination perform non-generic, technical functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory techniques courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically
rubrics_metrics.description: In the life sciences, courts have identified common laboratory techniques as well-understood, routine, conventional activities when recited at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: (i) determining the level of a biomarker in blood by any means; (ii) using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify and detect DNA; (iii) detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample; (iv) immunizing a patient against a disease; (v) analyzing DNA to provide sequence information or detect allelic variants; (vi) freezing and thawing cells; (vii) amplifying and sequencing nucleic acid sequences; and (viii) hybridizing a gene probe. These techniques, when claimed only generically, may be treated as routine and not contribute an inventive concept unless there is more specificity or an unconventional application/arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other activities courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond computer and lab functions, courts have treated certain everyday activities as routine when recited at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: (i) recording a customer’s order; (ii) shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards; (iii) restricting public access to media by requiring a consumer to view an advertisement; (iv) presenting offers and gathering statistics; (v) determining an estimated outcome and setting a price; and (vi) arranging a hierarchy of groups, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing information, and determining the price. As with other categories, being on this list does not automatically make every claim ineligible—context, specificity, and integration into a practical application matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations (beyond linking to a technological environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment to transform the judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaningful limitations can arise from considerations in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(d) when they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception or integrate it into a practical application. Examples: Diamond v. Diehr (use of Arrhenius equation integrated into an automated rubber-molding process — steps like installing rubber, measuring temperature, and automatically opening the press limited the mathematical equation to a practical application); Classen (analysis + a specific immunization step integrated the abstract analysis into a tangible treatment). By contrast, Alice found that recitation of a generic computer implementation merely linked an abstract idea to a technological environment and did not meaningfully limit it. Examiners must evaluate additional elements both individually and in combination—an element that is not enough alone may nonetheless be meaningful in combination (Diehr, BASCOM). For treatment/prophylaxis claims, overlap exists with Step 2A Prong Two considerations (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)(2)). When appropriate, examiners should explain on the record why additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception (the 'apply it' rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination whether additional elements are merely instructions to implement a judicial exception (i.e., 'apply it') or do more than recite using the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely state the judicial exception and add words that effectively say 'apply it' (or equivalent) do not render the exception patent-eligible. The Supreme Court requires that additional elements do 'more than simply stat[e] the [judicial exception] while adding the words ‘apply it’' (Alice quoting Mayo). Examples: Mayo—measuring metabolite levels was merely an instruction to apply the law of nature because measurement could be done by any means; Alice—recitation of a generic computer implementation was a mere instruction to apply an abstract idea; Benson—process for converting BCD to binary had no meaningful practical application except in connection with a computer. Requiring more than mere instructions does not mean claims must be narrow to be eligible: courts have found some broad claims eligible (e.g., McRO; Thales Visionix) and some narrow claims ineligible (e.g., Ultramercial; Electric Power Group). Examiners should beware of §101 analyses that turn on drafting (the 'draftsman’s art') and evaluate whether claimed additional elements supply a meaningful inventive concept beyond mere implementation.
